1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.name: Catalan Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.background: The Catalan is named after Catalonia: at the Barcelona tournament of 1929 the organisers asked Savielly Tartakower to create a new variation in homage to the region's chess history. It became part of the repertoire of leading players in the 1930s and 1940s, and Kramnik, Anand and Carlsen all used it in world championship games.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5.name: Catalan Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5.strategy: The classical reply: Black takes a stand in the centre and waits for the bishop to show its hand. The d5 pawn blocks the long diagonal for now, but Black will have to decide later whether to hold the centre or take on c4 and give the pawn back.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, before the fianchettoed bishop has done any work. Black steers for an unbalanced structure with a queenside pawn majority, in which White's fianchetto set-up is not very dangerous.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7.strategy: A quiet developing move: Black prepares to castle, commits to nothing and waits to see White's set-up. The bishop declines both a pin and a central strike, leaving Black solid but a step behind in the fight for space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+.strategy: Makes White decide how to block: a knight allows a pin, while the bishop ends up on d2, where it does little. Black aims to trade off a minor piece for a solid game; the main lines are drawish, though some sidelines are sharper.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 e5.name: Catalan Opening: Hungarian Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 e5.strategy: Throws the e-pawn forward at once, but White simply takes it, and after ...Ng4 attacks the pawn White can defend it. Black has given up a pawn for a little quick development, which is not enough.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2.strategy: Blocks the check with the bishop, attacking the undefended bishop on b4 and avoiding a pin on c3. The bishop is not ideally placed, but the move keeps the fianchetto plan intact and asks Black what to do with its bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Nc3.strategy: Blocks the check with the knight, which stays pinned on c3 until the king moves. Black can take it and double White's pawns, but White then has the two bishops and a half-open b-file; Black can also keep the pin and the tension. A sound trade of structure for piece activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Nd2.strategy: Blocks the check with the queen's knight, which then shuts in the bishop on c1 and the queen. If Black trades on d2, White recaptures with the bishop and keeps the two bishops, but development is slow and the bishop lands on a square that does little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7.strategy: Retreats instead of exchanging, so Black spends two moves with the bishop while White spent one. In return White's bishop stands on d2, where it takes the square from the b1 knight, and Black keeps all its pieces for a solid game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Qe7.strategy: Defends the bishop with the queen instead of retreating or trading it. If White exchanges on b4, Black recaptures with check and has lost nothing, so White's awkward bishop on d2 gains nothing. The cost is a queen committed early and a bishop that can no longer retreat to e7.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Bxd2+.strategy: Trades bishop for bishop at once, which removes the very problem White's last move created: the bishop on d2 is awkward, and the exchange takes it off the board. Black gets a quiet, safe game with few risks, but also few winning chances: it is mostly a way to draw.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at b7 and the centre, and White's king side is ready for castling. White now sets the pace, and Black must decide how to meet the pressure on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.N.strategy: Develops the king's knight before the bishop, guarding d4 and e5. After ...d5 the same set-up as with the bishop move arises; the difference is that Black has slightly more choice about when to play ...d5. The fianchetto stays in hand, so the queenside pressure is only delayed.

Develops the queen's knight at once, where it adds a second attacker to d5 once Black plays ...d5. It is sound, but it leaves the kingside bishop for later and lets Black set up with ...d5 and ...O-O comfortably, so White's pressure on the queenside builds slower than with the fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.strategy: Takes the centre and blocks the long diagonal for the moment. Black gets a solid pawn pair on d5 and e6 and a free path to castling, at the price of a cramped queen's bishop and a slightly passive game.

Castles first and keeps ...d5 in hand, so the pawn centre is not fixed before White shows its set-up. Black's king is safe and nothing is committed, but the long diagonal of White's bishop is already open and Black will have to answer it with ...d5 or ...c6 sooner or later.

Puts a pawn on the long diagonal to blunt White's bishop and prepares ...d5 behind a solid chain. Black gets a very sturdy centre, but the pawns on c6, d5 and e6 hem in the queen's bishop, and the slow move leaves Black passive while White develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Retreat Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.strategy: Completes the kingside development, guards d4 and e5 and prepares castling. White keeps the tension against d5 and c4, so the bishop on g2 keeps its influence and White presses for a small, lasting edge.

Puts the queen on its best square for this set-up: it defends c4, sees along the c-file and supports a later e4 advance. If Black takes on c4, the queen wins the pawn back at once. The knight on g1 still has to come out, but the queenside pressure is already in place.

Resolves the tension in the centre: Black recaptures and the pressure on d5 is gone for good. White gets a half-open c-file and the bishop on g2 still presses on d5, but the move trades the lasting queenside pressure for a quiet middlegame.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Retreat Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7 5.B.strategy: Brings the king to safety and finishes the kingside development. Black is compact and sturdy, though a little passive: White keeps the extra space and the long-term pressure on d5 and the queenside.

Develops the last minor piece to a square that supports a later central pawn break, but leaves the king in the centre a move longer. A reasonable alternative to castling, with the same solid but slightly cramped structure.

Takes on c4, trading the d5 pawn for White's c-pawn to free the game. White can win the c4 pawn back, but meanwhile Black escapes the cramped, passive set-up. The price is White's lead in development and the queenside pressure this set-up is built for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto at once. The bishop takes up the long diagonal and the pressure on the queenside, while Black's quiet bishop move has offered no target to attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and guards d4 and e5 before the bishop is placed. After ...d5 and Bg2 the main line arises by another move order; the only difference is that Black has a little more say in when ...d5 comes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, where it adds a second attacker to d5 after ...d5. It is sound but less precise: it stands in front of the c-pawn and takes the c-file away from a queen on c2, so the pressure on c4 and d5 is weaker than in the main set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre and shuts the long diagonal. Black builds a firm pawn pair on d5 and e6 and prepares to castle, content with a solid, somewhat cramped game while White decides how to keep up the pressure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Castles at once and leaves the centre pawns alone, so ...d5 can follow at any time. Black's king is safe and nothing is committed, but White's bishop already bears on the long diagonal and White gets time to build the position it prefers.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 c6.strategy: Blunts White's bishop on the long diagonal with a pawn and prepares ...d5. The chain on c6, d5 and e6 is very solid but hems in the queen's bishop, and Black spends a move without developing a piece while White continues freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops, guards the centre and prepares castling. Black keeps the d5 pawn as a strong point and will find the game closed and solid, while White keeps a slight space advantage and the pressure of the bishop on g2.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 d5 5.Qc2.strategy: Puts the queen on c2, where it defends c4, supports a later e4 advance and, if Black takes on c4, wins the pawn back along the file at once. The king's knight still has to come out, but the queenside pressure of the fianchetto is already in place.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 Be7 4.Bg2 d5 5.Nc3.strategy: Brings the knight to the centre, where it attacks d5 together with the bishop. It stands on the c-file in front of the c-pawn, so a queen on c2 would no longer see c4 if Black takes there. A sound developing move, but the pressure on the queenside is milder than in the main set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5.strategy: Gains space and fixes the centre at once, aiming at an unbalanced pawn structure. White holds the central pawns and may later push e4, while Black counters with a queenside majority and an open e-file.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and guards d4 and e5 without fixing the pawn structure, so White can still choose between releasing the central tension and holding it. A flexible alternative to gaining space at once, though Black then decides how the centre is settled.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto at once and lets Black decide the structure. If Black takes on d4, White can win the pawn back with Nf3 and Nxd4 while developing, and the bishop works on the long diagonal; the move is sound, but it leaves d4 to be defended later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the e-file against the pawn on e2. Black gives up the solid centre for activity: after the recapture White has the d5 pawn and central space, and Black plays for the queenside majority.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 d6.strategy: Declines to take on d5 and keeps the structure flexible. If White takes on e6, Black recaptures with the bishop, which develops with an attack on c4. The price is that White is not forced to resolve the centre and can keep its extra space, while Black's counterplay on the queenside comes more slowly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 b5.strategy: A gambit that offers the b-pawn to deflect White's c-pawn and build a broad pawn centre with ...exd5 or ...fxe6 and ...d5. It is offbeat: Black has to make up the pawn with activity, and White's bishop will soon bear on the centre, so the move is playable but second-rate.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cxd.strategy: Recaptures with the c-pawn, which gives White a pawn on d5 and a central majority but leaves Black the majority on the queenside. Each side now plays for its own pawn break in a sharp, unbalanced game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop but leaves the pawn on c4 attacked by the pawn on d5, with d4 also under fire from c5. Black takes on c4, and White has to spend time winning the pawn back, which is hard while d4 is also attacked.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.Qxd.strategy: Takes the pawn with the queen, but the pawn on d5 is defended by the knight on f6: 5...Nxd5 wins the queen, and the recapture 6.cxd5 returns only a knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cxd.strategy: Supports the c5 pawn, restrains White's e5 advance and frees the diagonal of the light-squared bishop. Black accepts White's space in return for the half-open e-file and a majority on the queenside.

Pushes the queenside majority at once to cramp White on that wing and open lines for the rooks. Black accepts a loose pawn on b5 and a looser structure for faster queenside play, instead of first stopping White's pawn on d5 from advancing to d6.

An eccentric development: the bishop supports c5 and blocks White's d-pawn on d6, but it takes the natural square from Black's own d-pawn and can be driven off by a central pawn advance. Playable, but less respected than the main line.

Develops the knight, defends d5 and prepares to build the centre with e4. White uses its space to prepare the push in the middle, while Black readies counterplay against the centre and on the queenside.

Develops the king's knight, which covers e5 and d4, before deciding where the queen's knight goes. With the fianchetto already in place the game typically becomes a slow one: White has more space and a safe king, Black the queenside majority and counterplay on the long diagonal.

Sets up the fianchetto before the knights move. The bishop guards d5 and keeps both squares of the queen's knight open, but it gives Black a free hand to organise play on the queenside, and a check on a5 forces White to react.

Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop on the long diagonal, from where it pressures the centre and the queenside. Black accepts White's centre and aims to undermine it, playing for dynamic counterplay along the e-file and the wing.

Prepares ...b5 to open the queenside, where Black has the majority, and takes the b5 square away from White's knight. Black delays the fianchetto in favour of queenside counterplay, which costs a move in development.

Develops the last minor piece, aiming for the e5 square that no white pawn guards. It shuts in the bishop on c8 and delays the fianchetto, so Black commits to a less direct set-up than the main line, though it remains sound.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop at once. It bears down the long diagonal on d5 and the queenside, and it leaves c4 loose on purpose: White is ready to win the pawn back if Black takes it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight first and reaches the same set-up by another move order. White guards d4 and e5, keeps the fianchetto in hand and waits to see whether Black takes on c4. It is a common way to reach the same position, and it gives Black the same choices.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and puts a second attacker on d5. The knight stands in front of the c-pawn and blocks the c-file, so the quiet pressure of the fianchetto and the idea of winning a captured pawn back along the file are gone. Sound, but less focused than the main set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4.background: An Open Catalan arose by transposition in Réti–Leonhardt, Berlin 1928, before Tartakower's usage at the Barcelona tournament.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the long diagonal for White's bishop. Black must either hold the extra pawn at the cost of weakening the queenside, or return it for time to develop. White gets lasting pressure and active pieces.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop, prepares castling and keeps the d5 strong point. Black avoids any commitment about c4 and accepts a solid, slightly cramped game in which White presses on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and keeps the centre tense. Black opens lines for the pieces, but may be left with a weak or isolated central pawn after the exchanges and must watch White's bishop on the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops, guards d4 against the pawn on c5 and prepares castling. White is ready to meet the tension in the centre with pieces rather than pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the tension in the centre and lets Black choose between recapturing with the pawn or the knight. Black's pawn on c5 now attacks d4, so White must watch that pawn, but the bishop on g2 looks down the long diagonal at the loosened position. A thematic, respectable alternative.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5 5.dxc5.strategy: Takes the c-pawn, but the pawn cannot be held: Black recovers it with ...Bxc5 or by pushing in the centre. White has given up the d4 pawn that held the centre, and Black develops freely while the bishop on g2 has less to press on.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5 5.Nf3.name: Catalan Opening: Tarrasch Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c5 5.Nf3.strategy: Adds a second attacker against d4 with a developing move. Black challenges the centre with pieces, and White must keep d4 under control while the long diagonal stays closed by the knight on f3.

Trades Black's c-pawn for White's d-pawn, opening the c-file for pressure on the queenside. White recaptures with the knight, which lands on a strong central square Black can challenge at once, but the d5 pawn is now exposed to the pawn on c4.

Takes the pawn and releases the central tension, but White regains it with check on a4 and the g2 bishop gets its long diagonal. Black has spent time on the pawn exchanges while the king is still in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.strategy: Develops and prepares castling without hurrying to regain the pawn. White relies on the bishop on g2 and a lead in development, and can win c4 back whenever it likes while Black has to find a plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Qa.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with check. The queen comes out early, but Black can hardly keep the pawn, so the game levels and White keeps the active bishop while Black gets easy development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Qc.strategy: Attacks c4 along the file but leaves the d4 pawn unguarded: Black takes it with the queen at once, and White must spend time chasing the queen away. The natural-looking move gives a pawn away for nothing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence, Classical Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.background: A favourite of Anatoly Karpov and Efim Geller as Black and of Oleg Romanishin as White.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.strategy: The classical set-up: Black develops, prepares to castle and expects to return the extra pawn. Without a pawn on d5, White's bishop hampers the queenside, and holding the pawn would force Black to weaken it badly.
Develops with an eye on d4 and the e5 square, but does little to protect the c4 pawn and walks into a queen move that pins the knight to the king. Active, but it puts Black's king under early strain.

Keeps the extra pawn: it prepares ...b5 and takes the b5 square away from White's queen. The price is the long diagonal, since once ...b5 is played and the knight on f3 steps aside, the g2 bishop hits the rook on a8, so Black must consolidate with care while White plays for development.
Attacks the c4 pawn and pins the knight on c6 to the king, so Black cannot defend the pawn with it. A sharp, direct try to win the pawn back while the king is still in the centre.

Castles first and leaves the c4 pawn for later. With queen and knight both guarding d4, ...Nxd4 simply loses a piece, so White can finish its development calmly; the cost is a move for Black to organise the defence of the extra pawn.

Develops a piece with influence over d5 and e4 and leaves the c4 pawn to be regained later. The delay costs a tempo: Black gets time to settle in and may keep the extra pawn a while longer, so the move is playable but not precise.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence, Modern Sharp Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Nf.strategy: Answers with check and blocks the queen's attack on c4. The bishop is guarded by the knight, so White cannot take it and must respond to the check. Black keeps the extra pawn for now and the game turns sharp.

Breaks the pin by interposing and accepts that White takes back on c4. Black gets harmonious development, but the bishop on d7 blocks Black's own queen on the d-file, so the centre needs watching until the bishop moves on.

A solid, passive way of returning the pawn: Black prepares to castle, which also frees the pinned knight, and White takes back on c4 with a small lead in activity. Black gets a safe king but little counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Qa.strategy: Blocks the check with a developing move, but the c4 pawn falls anyway. Black gives the pawn back in return for sound development and an equal, comfortable game.

Blocks the check with a pawn, which also closes the long diagonal for the g2 bishop. After White takes on c4 Black gains time with ...b5 against the queen, at the cost of a slightly passive development behind the c6 pawn.

Interposes with the bishop and lets the queen take on c4, after which the bishop can go to c6 to contest the long diagonal and blunt the g2 bishop. Black spends time on the manoeuvre but gets a sound, simple position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Qa.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4 5.Qa.strategy: Regains the pawn at once, so the g2 bishop gets its open long diagonal at no material cost. The price is a queen that has already moved twice and stands where Black's queenside pawns and knights can chase it, while Black has a free hand to organise.

Develops and prepares castling without hurrying to take on c4. While the queen pins the knight on d7 Black cannot defend the pawn with ...Nb6, so White can take it back whenever it likes, but the delay lets Black break the pin and gain time to organise.

Brings a piece out with influence over d5 and e4 and leaves the pawn on c4 to be regained later. Black gets time to break the pin and settle in, so White gives up the simplest way to regain the pawn for a more complicated game.

Takes b5 away from the queen and prepares to gain space and time with ...b5. The advance has to wait until Black has dealt with the long diagonal, because the b-pawn leaving b7 uncovers the rook on a8 to the bishop on g2.

Challenges d4 at once with the knight on d7 behind the pawn, aiming to trade off White's central pawn and free the game. It commits Black to an open centre in which the g2 bishop keeps pressing on b7, so Black must keep the queenside in order.

Hits the queen with a tempo and heads for d5, where the knight can block the long diagonal of the g2 bishop. Black gets a solid post for the knight, but the queen keeps its choice of good squares and stays active.
